description: We are a team of motivated and ambitious students passionate about technology, innovation, and solving real-world problems. Our main interests include computer science, artificial intelligence, software development, scientific research, and data-driven solutions. We aim to combine our creativity, technical knowledge, and diverse perspectives to develop practical projects that can make a meaningful impact.
summary: Aster is a free browser game for children aged 7–12, made for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It works offline from a single file. Players answer real science questions by running a space agency. In Act 1, they build rockets and fly them with realistic 2D physics: gravity, fuel, staging, drag and re-entry heating. They reach orbit, fly to the Moon and land, with guided practice flights and optional autopilot help. In Mission Control, starting from 1957, they choose science questions, design missions, build ground stations and satellites, research technology, and take on contracts and emergencies. They can also replay 16 real missions, from Sputnik to Europa Clipper, and compare their results with the real ones. A small machine-learning model, trained in the browser, predicts each mission’s chance of success. In Act 2, players keep a Moon outpost crew alive for 14 days. Real solar storms from NASA’s DONKI database and real ISS radiation readings from NASA RadLab affect what happens.
details:
Aster: Junior Space Program is a free browser game that teaches kids aged 7–12 how we reach space and how people survive there. It works offline from one HTML file, with no install or account.
How it works:
Act 1: Players build rockets and fly 9 missions in a real-physics simulator, from a first launch to orbit and a Moon landing.
Mission Control: Players run a space agency from 1957. They answer science questions with missions, build stations and satellites, and replay 16 real historical missions. A small machine-learning model predicts each mission’s chance of success.
Act 2: Players keep a Moon outpost crew alive for 14 days. Real NASA DONKI solar storms hit the base, and crew radiation is compared with real ISS readings from OSDR RadLab.
Impact: Kids learn about orbits, fuel and space radiation by trying, failing and trying again. Using real NASA data shows them how real science is done.
Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (Canvas 2D), with NASA open data: DONKI, OSDR, RadLab, JPL, NSSDCA and Blue Marble. [Name your AI tool here, or delete this sentence if you used none: “An AI assistant helped write parts of the code and text; our team designed, checked and tested everything.”]
Creativity: It’s one connected story, from building a rocket to running an agency to surviving on the Moon, using real solar storms. We kept it simple for kids, clearly labelled every data source, and made it work on any device.
